# The Lighthouse Keeper

The lighthouse stood alone on the rocky promontory, its white tower rising like a sentinel against the grey Atlantic. Thomas had kept the light for thirty-seven years, climbing the spiral stairs each evening to polish the great Fresnel lens and ensure it would shine through the darkness. His legs ached more with each passing season, but the rhythm of the work—the same steps, the same duties—had become the steady pulse of his life.

He'd arrived here as a young man, fresh from a failed apprenticeship in the city. The sea had called to him through books and dreams, and the lighthouse keepers guild had given him a chance. His wife, Margaret, had joined him in the keeper's cottage, and they'd raised two children in the shadow of the tower. Now those children had their own lives far away. Margaret rested in the graveyard beyond the birch grove. Thomas remained.

The automated warning system had arrived three years ago—a modern LED beacon that could operate itself. The authorities promised his job was safe until retirement, but Thomas knew better. Machines needed no food, no wages, and no company on long winter nights. He'd made peace with it. Every sunset, he still climbed the stairs. Every dawn, he descended them. These rituals mattered to him in a way he couldn't quite explain.
